full_judgment:
Sharifuddin Chaklader J: This Rule, at the instance of the accused petitioner, for quashing the judgment and order dated 22-11-2006 passed by the learned Additional Metropolitan. Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong convicting the accused petitioner under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of 1(one) month with a further direction to pay an amount of Taka 4,10,000 which includes compensation amounting to Taka 20,000 for the complainant cheque amount and Taka 20,000 for the State. 

 5. Mr Md Belayet Hossain, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that entire trial held by the learned Sessions Judge is vitiated as on the facts of given case the trial ought to be held by the learned Magistrate under the law prevailing when the offence was committed. Law was repealed on 9-6-2006. Learned Advocate further submits that it is settled principle of law that any amendment or the effect of any repelling' law applying prospectively as the case which was filed or which was initiated before repealing or amendment of law is to be governed by the old law not by the new law. Learned Advocate further submits that amendment as made, is not beneficial to the accused petitioner as in the present law a new clause has been inserted for paying 50% of the cheque amount for filing of appeal. From the side of the petitioner he case of Md Nazimuddin vs State, 30 DLR 49, the case of Muhammad vs State, PLD 1959 (WP) Karachi 94, Arshad Ali Sk vs Bangladesh, 29 DLR 301, Akhtar Hossain Khan vs State, 29 DLR (SC) 101 has been referred. 

 6. On the side of the complainant opposite party the case of Mohitullah Pk vs State, 38 DLR (AD) 240 has been cited. 

 10. In the case of Md Nizamuddin vs State, 30 DLR 49 where it was held that when a vested right has been accrued to an accused it cannot be taken away by subsequent amendment of the law. In that case, appellant Md Nizamuddin challenged the law of presenting the appeal to the Appellant Tribunal under section 30 of the Special Tribunal Act, 1974 as before insertion of section 30 of the Act appellant's right to presenting the appeal before the High Court Division was accrued and a vested right arising from the pending proceeding, In the case of Md Irtiza vs State, PLD 1959 (WP) Karachi, 94, the question raised is that after the commitment of the petitioners to Court of Sessions, case was initiated on 9-5-1954, by the learned Magistrate on 30-4- 1956 under section 167(G) of the Sea Customs Act, an amendment of section 3 of the Act was made on 2-8-1957 rendering the offences under section 167(G) of the Act triable by the Customs Authority. It was held that since the legal proceeding was instituted on 9-5-1954, will continue under the repealed provisions. In the case of Arshad Ali Sk vs Bangladesh, 29 DLR 301, where question arose whether after the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act and coming into force of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, an application for setting aside sale under section 173(4) of BT Act will lie. The application was filed on 2-11-66 for setting aside a sale held on 19-3-1952 in rent execution case No. 1308 of 1951. It was held that the application is maintainable In the case of Akhtar Hossain Khan vs State, 29 DLR (SC) 101 where the question mooted was that PO 50 of 1972 having been repealed on 9- 2-74 any police investigation in process before 9-2-74 in view of the decision in Mridha s case [26 DLR (SC) 17] could not be continued under PO 50, inasmuch as the saving clause under section 36(2)(b) of Special Powers Act has, provided fox the continuance of the cases that were pending under the said Act, and view of the aforementioned Mridhas decision the time at which cognisance of an offence under PO 50 commences is the date on which the charge sheet is submitted under Article 4of that Act and in the present case the Charge sheet was submitted when PO 50 was dead. It was held on reference to the case of Sona vs State, 22 DLR (SC) 155 that repeal of the Act shall not affect pending proceedings under it. Moreover, proceedings may be continued and punishment may be imposed as if repealing Act has not been passed. 

 11. On the other hand, Mohd Ziaul Haque, the learned Advocate for the complainant relied on the decisions of Mohitullah Pk vs State, 38 DLR (AD) 240 and Md Alam vs State, 19 DLR (SC) 213. The former case on relying the decision of the latter held that an accused shall be tried in accordance with the procedure prevailing on the day when the trial commenced and also held that if the procedure is changed by the time when the trial commences, the accused cannot claim a vested right to be tried in accordance with the procedure prevailing before that. 

 12. Now the question is, whether the amendment of Act is change of procedure or law. From a consideration of Section 138 of the Act at present .it is our considered view that it is a change of procedure giving jurisdiction to the Sessions Court to try the offence. Procedural law means to ensure that an accused gets a full and fair trial with notions of natural justice. Excepting the procedure as to holding of trial by Sessions Court instead of Magistracy the offence under section 138 of the Act remains same. In the decision of Mohd Alam vs State, supra, it has been held that if a statute deals merely with the procedure in an action and does not effect the rights of the parties, it will be held to apply prima-facie, to all actions pending as well as future. In the case of the State vs Ana Mia 1994 BLD (AD) 143 it is observed. It is true that with regard to procedural law the general principle is that alterations in procedure are retrospective unless  there is some good reasons against such a view. If a statute deals merely with the procedure in an action  and does not affect the rights 01 the parties, it will be  held to apply prima-facie to all actions pending as well as future.
